beats.narration_text: Namaste. I'm Liam, in for Kumar Karthik. For the last two weeks, Kumar has been rewriting one section of his review on machine learning for SERS: section four point four, on hybrid and multi-task architectures. So what actually changed? Three things.
Here's the whole update in one line. The draft said multi-task learning often helps, and cited nothing. The revision says it helps sometimes, and spells out exactly when.

The original section was two short paragraphs, and both of them mostly described. One model, one claim, one finding. The revision runs four paragraphs, and each one has a job: why the architecture was designed the way it was, evidence that cuts against the easy claim, the mechanism behind a result, and a rule readers can actually use.

production_viz.label: Before → After
production_viz.mechanic: 2 grey cards grow, then 4 ink cards grow, revised column framed in terracotta
production_viz.note: Paragraph roles paraphrase the change log; no figures on screen.

beats.narration_text: The biggest fix was a single sentence. The draft claimed joint training often improves both tasks, with no citation behind it. So Kumar looked for a controlled test. A twenty twenty-six preprint by Shamim and colleagues compared a multi-task model against the strongest single-task baseline, on a leakage-audited split. The multi-task model scored eighty-four point one two percent, and the single-task baseline was statistically indistinguishable.

production_viz.label: The Correction
production_viz.mechanic: Boxed quote, then backbone → two heads → results
production_viz.note: 84.12% and Tukey p = 1.0: AMTLNet vs CNN-LSTM single-task baseline, C-MAPSS FD001, leakage-audited split (Shamim et al. 2026, arXiv:2607.16493, abstract + Table 6). Different encoders, so NOT framed as identical-backbone.

beats.narration_text: That same study found something bigger. With naive splitting, accuracy on the same data and the same model swung anywhere from zero to ninety-nine point nine percent. The protocol mattered as much as the architecture. So the revision sets a default: when two tasks aren't naturally coupled, train one classifier and one regressor separately. They're easier to debug, and easier to interpret.

production_viz.label: Protocol, then default
production_viz.mechanic: Dot swinging on a 0–100% track, then a two-branch decision card
production_viz.note: Same data/model: IMS Bearing, Table 5 of Shamim et al. 2026. Naive window split 99.90%; degenerate split down to 0%; leakage-free refined split 30.00 ± 15.49%.

beats.narration_text: The autoencoder paragraph got its missing why. A model trained only to reconstruct a spectrum can hit that target with answers that are physically impossible, like negative concentrations. Building non-negativity into the model removes that failure. In wastewater, every spectrum is a mixture of contaminants, so an unmixing model that sometimes invents negative amounts isn't useful, however good its reconstruction looks.

production_viz.label: The missing why
production_viz.mechanic: Bar chart: negative concentration bars transform to non-negative
production_viz.note: Bar values are ILLUSTRATIVE, not from Georgiev et al. 2024; labeled on screen.

beats.narration_text: Here's the verdict. Section four point four now argues one principle: hybrid and multi-task models earn their complexity only when there's a structural reason, a real physical constraint, or two tasks that genuinely inform each other. And one housekeeping fix: reference U fifty-five now credits Georgiev and colleagues, published in P-N-A-S in twenty twenty-four.

artifactLines: Uncited multi-task claim replaced with a controlled, leakage-audited counterpoint.
Evaluation protocol shown to matter as much as architecture.
Two-model pipeline set as the default when tasks aren't naturally coupled.
ResFusionNet's design rationale added: dual-stream inputs and attention pooling.
Physics constraint explained: it blocks negative concentrations.
Citation [U-55] corrected to Georgiev et al., PNAS 2024.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick one model result you trust, and ask one question: was the data split by sample, or by spectrum? If you can't answer that, the accuracy number may not mean what you think it means.
